items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "Geiger–Marsden experiment".
items.answer: The scattering of alpha particles by thin gold foil, in which a small fraction were deflected through large angles
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the scattering of alpha particles by thin gold foil, in which a small fraction were deflected through large angles. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Hana writes: "The Geiger–Marsden experiment showed that electrons orbit in fixed shells." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It showed the existence of a small, dense, positive nucleus; electron energy levels came later from Bohr and spectroscopy.
items.markingKey: It showed the existence of a small, dense, positive nucleus; electron energy levels came later from Bohr and spectroscopy. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A teacher in Lisbon asks a class to choose the one correct statement about the nuclear model and Geiger-Marsden-Rutherford scattering. Which statement should be chosen?
options: Shorter-wavelength lines come from transitions with smaller energy differences.
Most passed straight through; only about 1 in 8000 was deflected through more than 90°.
Isotopes have the same mass number but different proton numbers.
The n = 2 level of hydrogen is at −6.8 eV.
items.answer: Most passed straight through; only about 1 in 8000 was deflected through more than 90°.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. Most passed straight through; only about 1 in 8000 was deflected through more than 90°.

items.stem: An α particle approaches a aluminium nucleus (Z = 13) and stops momentarily 9.35 × 10⁻¹⁵ m from it. What was its initial kinetic energy?
items.answer: 4.00 MeV
items.markingKey: B. Eₖ = k(2e)(Ze)/d = 4.00 MeV.

items.stem: An alpha particle of 4.0 MeV is fired directly at a gold nucleus (Z = 79). What is the distance of closest approach?
items.markingKey: A. d = k(2e)(79e)/Eₖ = 5.68 × 10⁻¹⁴ m; using charge e instead of 2e gives half this.

items.stem: In a modern version of the Geiger–Marsden experiment, 5.5 MeV alpha particles are scattered by thin gold foil. (a) Calculate the distance of closest approach for a head-on collision. (b) Compare this with the radius of a gold nucleus (A = 197) from R = R₀A^(1/3). (c) Predict and explain what would be observed if the alpha energy were raised to 30 MeV.
items.answer: (a) d = k(2e)(79e)/Eₖ = 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m; (b) R = 1.20 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 197^(1/3) = 7.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ m – the alpha particle stays well outside the nucleus, so pure Coulomb (Rutherford) scattering is observed; (c) at 30 MeV d ≈ 7.6 fm, comparable to R, so the alpha reaches the strong-force range and deviations from Rutherford’s formula appear at large angles, revealing the nuclear size.
items.markingKey: (a) d = k(2e)(79e)/Eₖ = 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m; (b) R = 1.20 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 197^(1/3) = 7.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ m – the alpha particle stays well outside the nucleus, so pure Coulomb (Rutherford) scattering is observed; (c) at 30 MeV d ≈ 7.6 fm, comparable to R, so the alpha reaches the strong-force range and deviations from Rutherford’s formula appear at large angles, revealing the nuclear size.

items.stem: Why was the gold foil in the Geiger–Marsden experiment made very thin?

items.answer: reduce the fraction scattered through large angles
items.markingKey: D. Weaker repulsion from smaller nuclear charge.

items.stem: Briefly explain why high-energy electrons, rather than alpha particles, are used to measure nuclear radii accurately.
items.answer: Electrons are not affected by the strong nuclear force, so they probe the charge distribution cleanly; at high energy their de Broglie wavelength is ~10⁻¹⁵ m, comparable to nuclei, giving a diffraction minimum from which the radius is found.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Electrons are not affected by the strong nuclear force, so they probe the charge distribution cleanly; at high energy their de Broglie wavelength is ~10⁻¹⁵ m, comparable to nuclei, giving a diffraction minimum from which the radius is found. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the plum-pudding model and the nuclear model.
items.answer: The plum-pudding model spreads positive charge throughout the atom with embedded electrons; the nuclear model concentrates the positive charge and nearly all the mass in a tiny nucleus with electrons outside.
items.markingKey: The plum-pudding model spreads positive charge throughout the atom with embedded electrons; the nuclear model concentrates the positive charge and nearly all the mass in a tiny nucleus with electrons outside. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The Geiger–Marsden experiment is a good example of how unexpected results drive scientific change."
items.answer: Yes: an anomalous result led to a paradigm shift, but it required careful theory and further revision (NOS).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: large-angle scattering contradicted the accepted model and led to the nuclear model. Arguments against: the model still had problems (electron stability) that required quantum theory; Rutherford’s mathematical analysis, not just the observation, was crucial. Supported judgement: Yes: an anomalous result led to a paradigm shift, but it required careful theory and further revision (NOS). items.stem: A student wants to test the relationship R = R₀A^(1/3) for nuclear radii measured by electron scattering. State which quantities should be plotted on the axes to obtain a straight-line graph, and state what the gradient represents.
items.answer: Plot R (y-axis) against A^(1/3) (x-axis); gradient = R₀ (about 1.2 fm). A straight line through the origin confirms constant nuclear density.
items.markingKey: Correct choice of axes: R against A^(1/3) (M1); straight line expected (R1); gradient = R₀ (about 1.2 fm) (A1). A straight line through the origin confirms constant nuclear density.

items.stem: Explain the difference between isotopes and isobars (same A, different Z).
items.answer: Isotopes have the same Z but different A (same element); nuclides with the same A but different Z are different elements with similar masses.

Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The formula R = R₀A^(1/3) shows that nuclei are hard spheres with sharp edges."
items.answer: The formula is an excellent approximation for the average size but nuclei have diffuse surfaces and can be non-spherical.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it fits electron-scattering data well; it implies constant density. items.stem: Show that the density of nuclear matter is independent of nucleon number using R = R₀A^(1/3), and calculate it (R₀ = 1.20 fm, nucleon mass ≈ 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg). Then estimate the radius a sphere of nuclear density would have if it contained the mass of Earth (5.97 × 10²⁴ kg).
items.answer: ρ = A m_u/((4/3)πR₀³A) = 3m_u/(4πR₀³) = 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, independent of A. Radius: (3M/(4πρ))^(1/3) = (3 × 5.97 × 10²⁴/(4π × 2.3 × 10¹⁷))^(1/3) ≈ 180 m.
items.markingKey: ρ = A m_u/((4/3)πR₀³A) = 3m_u/(4πR₀³) = 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, independent of A. Radius: (3M/(4πρ))^(1/3) = (3 × 5.97 × 10²⁴/(4π × 2.3 × 10¹⁷))^(1/3) ≈ 180 m.

items.stem: Electrons of energy 420 MeV are diffracted by oxygen-16 nuclei and the first diffraction minimum is observed at about 44°. (a) Show that the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons is about 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ m (treat them as ultra-relativistic, E = pc). (b) Using sin θ ≈ 1.22λ/(2R), estimate the nuclear radius. (c) Compare with R = R₀A^(1/3) and comment.
items.answer: (a) p = E/c = 420 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹/3.00 × 10⁸ = 2.24 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹; λ = h/p = 2.96 × 10⁻¹⁵ m; (b) R = 1.22λ/(2 sin 44°) = 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ m; (c) R₀A^(1/3) = 1.20 × 16^(1/3) = 3.0 fm – the same order, agreeing within the approximations.
items.markingKey: p = E/c (M1); λ = h/p ≈ 3.0 fm (A1); R ≈ 2.6 fm (M1 A1); comparison and comment on approximations (R1).

items.stem: Explain the difference between ground state and excited state.
items.answer: The ground state is the lowest energy level of the atom; an excited state is any higher level, from which the electron returns by emitting photons.

items.stem: Explain why absorption lines are dark even though the excited atoms re-emit photons.
items.answer: Re-emission occurs in random directions, so very little of the absorbed light continues towards the observer along the original beam; the line therefore appears dark relative to the continuum.

items.stem:
The wavelengths λ of four visible lines of the hydrogen (Balmer) series, ending on n = 2, are measured with a spectrometer. Theory: 1/λ = R_H(1/4 − 1/n²).

n / – | λ / nm
6 | 410.2
5 | 433.7
4 | 485.3
3 | 657.2

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the Rydberg constant R_H. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±2 %. State R_H with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) 1/λ in m⁻¹ (y) against (1/4 − 1/n²) (x); (b) gradient ≈ 1.10 × 10⁷ m⁻¹; (c) 1.10 × 10⁷ m⁻¹; (d) 1.10 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ ± 2 × 10⁵ m⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) 1/λ in m⁻¹ (y) against (1/4 − 1/n²) (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 1.10 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) R_H = gradient = 1.10 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 2 % of the value = 2 × 10⁵ m⁻¹; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: A fluorescent tube contains mercury vapour. Electrons in the discharge excite mercury atoms, which emit ultraviolet at 254 nm; a phosphor coating then emits visible light. (a) Calculate the energy of a 254 nm photon in eV. (b) Explain why the phosphor emits light of longer wavelength than it absorbs. (c) Explain why the light from the tube is not a continuous spectrum and why this affects how colours look.
items.answer: (a) E = hc/λ = 7.83 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 4.89 eV; (b) the phosphor atoms are raised to a high level and return in several smaller steps, each emitting a lower-energy (longer-wavelength) photon; (c) emission is from discrete level differences in the phosphors, so the spectrum consists of bands/lines; objects reflecting wavelengths absent from the spectrum appear different (poor colour rendering).
items.markingKey: E = hc/λ (M1) 4.89 eV (A1); cascade through intermediate levels (R1); discrete energy levels give line/band spectrum (R1); colour rendering consequence (R1).

items.stem: According to the Bohr model, what is the energy of the hydrogen electron in the n = 3 level?

(a) Show that the Bohr condition mvr = nh/2π combined with ke²/r² = mv²/r gives rₙ ∝ n². (b) Show that the total energy of the electron is E = −ke²/(2r). (c) Hence explain why Eₙ ∝ −1/n² and calculate E₁ given r₁ = 5.29 × 10⁻¹¹ m.
items.answer: (a) v = nh/(2πmr); substituting into mv² = ke²/r gives r = n²h²/(4π²mke²) ∝ n²; (b) Eₖ = ½mv² = ke²/(2r), Eₚ = −ke²/r, total −ke²/(2r); (c) E ∝ −1/r ∝ −1/n²; E₁ = −8.99 × 10⁹ × (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)²/(2 × 5.29 × 10⁻¹¹) = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J = −13.6 eV.
items.markingKey: Substitution for v (M1); r ∝ n² (A1); Eₖ and Eₚ (M1); total energy (A1); E₁ = −13.6 eV (A1).

items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: It showed the existence of a small, dense, positive nucleus; electron energy levels came later from Bohr and spectroscopy.

items.stem: Explain why all nuclei have approximately the same density.
items.answer: Volume ∝ R³ = R₀³A, and mass ≈ A × u, so density = mass/volume ≈ 3u/(4πR₀³), independent of A; nucleons pack together at constant spacing.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Volume ∝ R³ = R₀³A, and mass ≈ A × u, so density = mass/volume ≈ 3u/(4πR₀³), independent of A; nucleons pack together at constant spacing. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how the Bohr condition mvr = nh/2π can be interpreted using de Broglie waves.
items.answer: Using λ = h/(mv), the condition becomes 2πr = nλ: a whole number of electron wavelengths fits around the orbit, forming a standing wave, so only these orbits are stable.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Using λ = h/(mv), the condition becomes 2πr = nλ: a whole number of electron wavelengths fits around the orbit, forming a standing wave, so only these orbits are stable. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why the dark lines in an absorption spectrum occur at the same wavelengths as the bright lines in the emission spectrum of the same element.
items.answer: Both correspond to transitions between the same pairs of energy levels; a photon of energy ΔE = hc/λ is absorbed to raise an electron and emitted when it falls back, so the wavelengths coincide.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Both correspond to transitions between the same pairs of energy levels; a photon of energy ΔE = hc/λ is absorbed to raise an electron and emitted when it falls back, so the wavelengths coincide. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Estimate the minimum kinetic energy, in MeV, an alpha particle would need to reach the surface of a platinum nucleus (Z = 78, A = 197), using R = R₀A^(1/3) with R₀ = 1.20 fm.
items.answer: 32.1 MeV

items.stem: Hana writes: "A heavier nucleus is denser than a lighter one." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Nuclear density is roughly constant (~2 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³) for all nuclei.
items.markingKey: Nuclear density is roughly constant (~2 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³) for all nuclei. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Calculate the energy needed to ionise a hydrogen atom whose electron is in the n = 4 level, in eV and in J.
items.markingKey: Eₙ = −13.6/4² = −0.850 eV (M1); ionisation energy = 0.850 eV = 1.36 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (A1).

items.stem: An electron falls between two energy levels separated by 1.89 eV. What is the wavelength of the emitted photon?
items.answer: 658 nm

items.stem: An alpha particle of 8.0 MeV is fired directly at a gold nucleus (Z = 79). What is the distance of closest approach?
items.markingKey: C. d = k(2e)(79e)/Eₖ = 2.84 × 10⁻¹⁴ m; using charge e instead of 2e gives half this.

items.stem: Calculate the radius of the nucleus of ¹H, using R = R₀A^(1/3) with R₀ = 1.20 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.
Elena writes: "In the Bohr model the electron radiates energy continuously as it orbits." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Bohr postulated that electrons in allowed orbits do NOT radiate; photons are emitted only during transitions between orbits.
items.markingKey: Bohr postulated that electrons in allowed orbits do NOT radiate; photons are emitted only during transitions between orbits. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Spectroscopy is the most important source of information about stars."
items.answer: Spectroscopy is arguably the richest single source, but it must be combined with other methods to determine distance and mass.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: gives composition, temperature, radial velocity, magnetic fields; works at any distance. Arguments against: distances need parallax or standard candles; masses need binary orbits; luminosity needs brightness and distance. Supported judgement: Spectroscopy is arguably the richest single source, but it must be combined with other methods to determine distance and mass.

items.stem: Describe the Geiger–Marsden experiment and explain how the observations led to the nuclear model of the atom. Include the purpose of each part of the apparatus and the significance of the angular distribution of scattered alpha particles.
items.answer: A collimated beam of alpha particles from a radium source in an evacuated chamber struck thin gold foil; a zinc sulfide screen viewed by microscope was moved around to count scintillations at different angles. Most particles passed undeviated (atom mostly empty), some were deflected through small angles, and about 1 in 8000 through more than 90° (concentrated positive charge and mass). Rutherford showed the number scattered at angle θ follows 1/sin⁴(θ/2), consistent with a Coulomb force from a point-like nucleus of radius < 10⁻¹⁴ m.
items.markingKey: Source, collimation, vacuum, thin foil, ZnS detector (A1 A1); three observations with interpretation (R1 R1 R1); quantitative angular distribution / size estimate (A1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "A neutron star can be thought of as a giant atomic nucleus."
items.answer: The density comparison is apt, but the binding mechanism differs, so the analogy is partial.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: density ~10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, similar to nuclear density; made mostly of neutrons held at nuclear separations. Arguments against: it is bound by gravity, not the strong force; contains electrons, protons and possibly exotic matter; its radius (~10 km) does not follow R₀A^(1/3) scaling physics in the same way. Supported judgement: The density comparison is apt, but the binding mechanism differs, so the analogy is partial. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: "The success of the Bohr model for hydrogen proves that electrons orbit the nucleus in circles." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: No: correct predictions support but do not prove a model; the orbit picture was replaced by wavefunctions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it reproduces the hydrogen energy levels exactly. Arguments against: it fails for multi-electron atoms and fine structure; quantum mechanics gives the same energies without definite orbits; agreement of predictions does not prove the mechanism (NOS). Supported judgement: No: correct predictions support but do not prove a model; the orbit picture was replaced by wavefunctions. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A set of discrete bright lines of specific wavelengths emitted by a hot, low-pressure gas"?
items.answer: emission spectrum
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of emission spectrum.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The minimum separation between an alpha particle and a nucleus in a head-on collision, where all its kinetic energy has become electric potential energy"?
items.answer: distance of closest approach
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of distance of closest approach.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "nucleon number (mass number) A".
items.answer: The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the quantum-mechanical model and the Bohr model.
items.answer: The Bohr model has definite circular orbits with quantised angular momentum; quantum mechanics replaces orbits with probability distributions (orbitals) given by wavefunctions and applies to all atoms.
items.markingKey: The Bohr model has definite circular orbits with quantised angular momentum; quantum mechanics replaces orbits with probability distributions (orbitals) given by wavefunctions and applies to all atoms. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which of the following statements about emission and absorption spectra and atomic energy levels is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Chloé.)
options: An atom can absorb a photon of any energy to raise an electron to a higher level.
Nuclear density is roughly constant (~2 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³) for all nuclei.
Isotopes have the same proton number but different numbers of neutrons, so different mass numbers.
E = hc/λ: shorter wavelength means larger energy difference.
items.answer: An atom can absorb a photon of any energy to raise an electron to a higher level.
items.markingKey: A. This is incorrect: A photon is absorbed only if its energy exactly matches the difference between two levels (or exceeds the ionisation energy).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the distance of closest approach gives only an upper limit for the radius of the nucleus.
items.answer: At closest approach the alpha particle is still outside the nucleus (it has been repelled by the Coulomb force without touching), so the nuclear radius must be smaller than this distance, unless deviations from Rutherford scattering are seen.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: At closest approach the alpha particle is still outside the nucleus (it has been repelled by the Coulomb force without touching), so the nuclear radius must be smaller than this distance, unless deviations from Rutherford scattering are seen. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In an investigation the relationship R = R₀A^(1/3) for nuclear radii, tested using logarithms is expected. Explain how a linear graph can be used to verify this relationship and to determine a value from the gradient.
items.answer: Plot ln R (y-axis) against ln A (x-axis); gradient = 1/3 (the power), with intercept ln R₀. A gradient of 1/3 confirms the cube-root dependence.
items.markingKey: Correct choice of axes: ln R against ln A (M1); straight line expected (R1); gradient = 1/3 (the power), with intercept ln R₀ (A1). A gradient of 1/3 confirms the cube-root dependence.

items.stem: A student in Nairobi is checking notes on Bohr model for hydrogen (HL). Which statement is incorrect?
options: Isotopes have the same proton number but different numbers of neutrons, so different mass numbers.
Nuclear density is roughly constant (~2 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³) for all nuclei.
The n = 2 level of hydrogen is at −6.8 eV.
Most passed straight through; only about 1 in 8000 was deflected through more than 90°.
items.answer: The n = 2 level of hydrogen is at −6.8 eV.
items.markingKey: C. This is incorrect: E₂ = −13.6/2² = −3.4 eV.

items.stem: White light passes through cool sodium vapour. The spectrum observed shows
options: bright sodium lines on a dark background
a continuous spectrum with dark lines at sodium wavelengths
items.answer: a continuous spectrum with dark lines at sodium wavelengths
items.markingKey: D. Absorption spectrum.

items.stem: In a head-on collision with a platinum nucleus an alpha particle of 4.8 MeV comes within 4.67 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Determine the energy needed to come within 2.34 × 10⁻¹⁴ m, and explain the reasoning.
items.answer: 9.60 MeV
items.markingKey: Eₖ = kqQ/d, so Eₖ ∝ 1/d (R1); halving d needs twice the energy: 9.60 MeV (A1).

items.stem:
The wavelengths λ of four visible lines of the hydrogen (Balmer) series, ending on n = 2, are measured with a spectrometer. Theory: 1/λ = R_H(1/4 − 1/n²).

n / – | λ / nm
6 | 409.6
5 | 434.6
4 | 486.1
3 | 655.2

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]

(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State R_H with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) 1/λ in m⁻¹ (y) against (1/4 − 1/n²) (x); (b) gradient ≈ 1.10 × 10⁷ m⁻¹; (c) 1.10 × 10⁷ m⁻¹; (d) 1.10 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ ± 4 × 10⁵ m⁻¹

items.stem: "Rutherford’s nuclear model was the final correct model of the atom." Discuss.
items.answer: It was a major step but not final; models are refined as evidence accumulates (NOS).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explained large-angle scattering and introduced the nucleus. Arguments against: could not explain atomic stability or line spectra; Bohr and then quantum mechanics replaced electron orbits; the nucleus itself has structure (protons, neutrons, quarks). Supported judgement: It was a major step but not final; models are refined as evidence accumulates (NOS). Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The formula R = R₀A^(1/3) shows that nuclei are hard spheres with sharp edges."
items.answer: The formula is an excellent approximation for the average size but nuclei have diffuse surfaces and can be non-spherical.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it fits electron-scattering data well; it implies constant density. Arguments against: scattering shows a diffuse surface region about 2 fm thick; R₀ differs slightly for charge and matter radii; nuclei may be deformed. Supported judgement: The formula is an excellent approximation for the average size but nuclei have diffuse surfaces and can be non-spherical. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: "The Bohr model should no longer be taught because it is wrong." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It should be taught as a historically important, limited model, with its limitations made explicit.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: orbits are not real; electrons are described by wavefunctions. Arguments against: it gives correct energy levels for hydrogen with simple mathematics; it introduces quantisation and shows how models evolve (NOS); it is a useful stepping stone. Supported judgement: It should be taught as a historically important, limited model, with its limitations made explicit.
